analysis.tldr: Dearer crude oil means India will likely pay more for imported fuel, pushing up everyday inflation and putting pressure on the rupee.
the_story: Brent crude (global oil benchmark) rose 13.6% in October to settle at $117.64 a barrel, hitting a six-month high.
The price jump was driven by fears of fresh US strikes on Iran and potential threats to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Analysts, including Goldman Sachs, warn of further market swings and flag a possible rise in oil prices to $120 a barrel.
analysis.what_happened: Global oil prices surged because traders worried that military action by the US against Iran and disruptions in crucial shipping lanes could choke off oil supplies. When supply looks uncertain, prices naturally shoot up.
analysis.analogy: It is like a major neighborhood grocery supplier facing delivery blockades; suddenly everyone rushes to buy stock, and the price of essentials goes up for everyone.
why_it_matters_india: Global oil prices jump due to supply fears in the Middle East.
India imports a large share of its crude oil, so buying it becomes more expensive for the country.
Higher import bills mean India needs more US dollars, causing the rupee to weaken (each rupee buys fewer dollars).
Costlier crude translates to higher domestic fuel and transport costs, raising overall inflation (general rise in prices) for everyday consumers.

impacts.rationale: More expensive crude oil makes producing fuel costlier, which usually leads to higher prices at the pump — bad for household budgets.
India needs more dollars to pay for costlier oil imports, weakening the local currency — bad for anyone buying imported goods or travelling abroad.
Higher transport and energy costs make everyday goods and services more expensive — bad for ordinary consumers.

watch_next: Developments regarding US military actions and political statements concerning Iran
Shipping traffic updates through the Strait of Hormuz
analysis.caveats: If tensions in the Middle East ease suddenly, oil prices could reverse quickly.

events.article_text:
Chevron Profits Nearly Triple to $9.9 Billion

Speculative positioning is already extremely…

Tom majored in International Business at Amsterdam’s Higher School of Economics and later completed an Executive MBA in Energy Transition at the University of Groningen.…

Fears of renewed U.S.-Iran hostilities are intensifying, with rising Hormuz attacks, reported explosions at Iran's Jask port and military repositioning overshadowing diplomatic efforts.

With only several days left until the US midterm elections, oil prices are set for a hefty 13-14% month-on-month increase as ICE Brent trends around $118 per barrel. Qatari and Pakistani mediation notwithstanding, everything is pointing towards a resumption in US-Iran hostilities in the upcoming weeks – rising numbers of Hormuz attacks, reported explosions at Iran’s Jask port, reports of military repositioning as well as extremely bullish CTA positioning. The markets should brace for a set of extremely volatile trading sessions next week…

War Turns Refining into Big Oil’s Profit Engine. US oil majors ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM) and Chevron (NYSE:CVX) both beat analyst expectations for Q3 profits, cashing in $15.4 billion and $9.9 billion respectively, with Exxon earning more from downstream than upstream for the first time in six years.

Iran Claims Three Tankers Struck Hormuz Mines. Iran’s IRGC said three unidentified vessels struck naval mines, caught fire and were abandoned after using an “unauthorised” route and ignoring Tehran’s warnings, whilst the US Centcom disputes claims that the strait’s main shipping lane has been mined.

Europe Taps SPRs to Cool Diesel Prices. EU governments will release 42 million barrels of strategic oil and product reserves over the next three months—half of it diesel—with France expecting pump-price relief of €0.12-0.18 per litre ($0.51-0.76 per gallon) within days after its 10-million-barrel release.

Saudi Oil Pitches Discounted Crude to Europe. Saudi national oil firm Saudi Aramco (TADAWUL:2222) reportedly started offering discounted spot cargoes for October and November arrival to European buyers, seeking to maximize loadings through the Red Sea coast, in avoidance of the Houthis.

ADNOC Pushes Toward Zero Reliance on Hormuz. Abu Dhabi’s national oil company ADNOC has told its clients that the second 1.5 million b/d pipeline to Fujairah, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, would see first deliveries in early 2027, seeking to reduce transits of its offshore grades to a bare minimum.

Compressor Failure Disrupts US Butane Exports. US refining giant Phillips 66 (NYSE:PSX) declared force majeure on butane loadings from its 260,000 b/d Freeport LPG terminal after a power outage and compressor failure, risking supply as US facilities operate at high rates to meet strong export demand.

Buoyed by Record Margins, Valero Revives Houston Capacity. US refiner Valero Energy (NYSE:VLO) has agreed to buy LyondellBasell’s idled Houston refinery for $320 million and restart its 165,000 b/d distillation column by end-2027, defying calls to restart its 145,000 b/d Benicia plant in California.

Russia Keeps Its Diesel Ban, Creates Caveat for US Exports. Moscow plans to extend diesel export restrictions through January while granting separate quotas for US-bound cargoes that could lift November shipments to 2.15 million tonnes and potentially 3.5 million tonnes by year-end.

Egypt Turns to Fuel Oil as Its LNG Bill Surges. Egypt’s state energy company EGPC bought six fuel oil cargoes for November–December delivery as soaring LNG prices threaten the country’s finances as Cairo budgeted $10.1 for LNG imports in financial year 2026/2027, having already spent 60% of the sum.

Europe Gas Crisis Deepens as Iran Risks Return. TTF, Europe’s natural gas benchmark, soared past €100 per MWh ($34 per MMBtu) and is heading for a 42% monthly gain as European inventories started net withdrawals even though storage sites are only 75% full, further buoyed by the risk of US-Iran hostilities.

Chile’s Copper Slump Deepens Global Squeeze. Chile’s Q3 copper output slumped 12% year-on-year to 1.16 million tonnes, the lowest production level in at least two decades, driven lower by recurring mining accidents, inclement weather, operational problems and declining ore grades.

Armed Group Again Disrupts Libya’s Oil Lifeline. Libya’s NOC reported another incident when an armed group shut a valve on the Hamada-Zawiya pipeline, halting flows to the 120,000 b/d Zawiya refinery – the country’s largest - highlighting persistent security risks to the country’s oil-dependent economy.

Asia Fuel-Oil Spreads Hit Records as Freight Costs Surge. The east-west pricing spread for fuel oil ballooned to a record high in Asia this week, as record freight costs from Europe pushed the November 380-cst high-sulphur spread to $155 per tonne with the low-sulphur spread topping $200 per tonne.

Japan to Reclaim LNG Import Crown from China. Japan is set to reclaim the LNG import crown from China this year, taking in 62 million tonnes whilst Chinese imports are expected to slump to 61 million tonnes, as mild winter expectations, almost-full Chinese storage and higher prices suppress demand.

China’s Aluminium Boom Moves Abroad. Chinese aluminium producers are expanding across Asia and Africa in a bid to expand smelting capacity as Beijing’s 45-million-tonne capacity regulatory cap is pushing investment abroad, with at least 15 mtpa of new capacity planned or recently announced.

analysis.tldr: Rising tensions between the US and Iran are pushing global oil prices close to $120 a barrel, which makes importing energy costlier for India and threatens to push up everyday prices at home.
the_story: ICE Brent crude oil is trading around $118 per barrel, heading for a 13-14% month-on-month increase driven by fears of renewed US-Iran hostilities.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard reported that three unidentified vessels struck naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, while the US Central Command disputes that the main shipping lane is mined.
US oil majors ExxonMobil and Chevron reported massive Q3 profits of $15.4 billion and $9.9 billion respectively, benefiting heavily from high refining margins.
European governments plan to release 42 million barrels of strategic oil reserves over the next three months to cool surging diesel prices.
analysis.what_happened: Global oil prices are surging toward $120 a barrel because fears of military conflict between the US and Iran are disrupting the Middle East. Reports of naval mine explosions in the Strait of Hormuz (a crucial narrow sea channel for oil tankers) and military repositioning have spooked traders, causing oil supplies to look tight.
analysis.analogy: It is like a major highway carrying all the fruit trucks to your city suddenly having security checkpoints and closures, causing fruit prices at your local market to shoot up instantly.
why_it_matters_india: Conflict and rising tension in the Middle East threaten major oil shipping routes like the Strait of Hormuz.
Global crude oil prices (ICE Brent) rise toward $120 per barrel.
Because India imports most of its oil, the country has to pay significantly more dollars to buy it.
This drives up domestic fuel costs, increases imported inflation (general rise in prices), and puts pressure on the Indian rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars).

impacts.rationale: Directly driven by supply fears and military tensions in the Middle East — makes importing energy more expensive for India.
India needs more dollars to buy costlier oil, which weakens the rupee — bad for ordinary citizens as imports become pricier.
Costlier crude filters through to transport and manufacturing, raising everyday consumer prices — bad for household budgets.
Global investors flock to safe assets during military tensions, lifting gold prices — mixed for buyers, good for existing holders.

Whether other major oil-producing nations decide to pump more oil to calm the market
analysis.caveats: If unexpected diplomatic breakthroughs ease Middle East tensions quickly, oil prices could reverse course and drop sharply.

events.headline: Will Fed chair Kevin Warsh’s AI optimism put him in a corner if the sector stalls?

items.title: Will Fed chair Kevin Warsh’s AI optimism put him in a corner if the sector stalls?
items.summary: The American central bank’s decision to pause rates has merit, but a quarter-point rate increase in December would be prudent. It’s concerning to think the Fed chair may have cornered himself into overreacting to an AI wobble and abandoning the possibility of further rate hikes.

events.article_text:
US Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh champions parsimony in central bank communications and loathes so-called forward guidance. But he’s said plenty about the future of artificial intelligence (AI): He’s an arch optimist on the technology who thinks it will help him vanquish inflation.

In a November Wall Street Journal column published shortly before getting picked to lead the central bank, Warsh wrote that “AI will be a significant disinflationary force, increasing productivity and bolstering American competitiveness.”

So how will he react if the AI boom stalls, as more now predict with evidence emerging that the sector may be facing a budding funding crunch?

It’s concerning to think that Warsh may have boxed himself into overreacting to such a wobble and abandoning the possibility of further interest-rate increases. Fed-watchers may have gotten a taste of his views Wednesday at what markets broadly perceived as a dovish press conference following the Federal Open Market Committee’s decision to keep rates steady at 3.75%-4%.

The Bloomberg Artificial Intelligence Index of 50 notable AI developers, facilitators and users dropped as much as 10% this month, amid concern that revenue growth might slow from spectacular to simply great, and that data centre companies might struggle to keep financing their expansions as borrowing costs rise. Debt yields surged for CoreWeave, the AI cloud-computing provider, and data centre peers with growth models that are dependent on borrowing at a reasonable price.

As I’ve noted earlier, the recent turbulence calls for a cautious approach to monetary policy that guards against the possibility that this trickle of credit stress becomes a flood, and the Fed was right to take a break from increasing rates this month. But caution doesn’t mean capitulating to inflation that’s been above the Fed’s 2% target for almost six years. Warsh should still aim to shepherd policymakers toward a quarter-point hike in December.

In some ways, an AI wobble might have a silver lining for monetary policy. Warsh’s disinflationary thesis on AI is fundamentally a long-run bet even though AI is clearly adding to inflation at the moment.

The high bandwidth memory that AI companies have gorged on soaks up a massive amount of the wafer space that the memory industry produces, much of which would typically go to conventional memory for personal devices. Personal computers and peripheral equipment prices are up 9.7% in the past year. To quote Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia President Anna Paulson: “While the impact of AI on productivity remains unclear, its effect on prices is not.”

If you get AI companies to pump the brakes in a meaningful way, wafer availability will improve and inflation could cool in related categories. And most Americans would be none the worse for it.

A slowdown would hurt the famously boom-and-bust semiconductor industry, but new specialized factories, known as fabs, are already underway and poised to arrive in 2027 and 2028, including those from Micron Technology and SK Hynix.

Warsh seemed to at least entertain the possibility on Wednesday that the Fed’s quarter-point rate increase in September is already bringing supply and demand into better balance.

Asked at his press conference whether the Fed might already be at the “right” policy setting, bond markets read his hemming and hawing as a maybe, with the yield on the two-year Treasury note dropping as much as 11 basis points in intraday trading.

“Well, we’ve got to determine the appropriate protocol,” Warsh said. “If you were listening next to me in that room the last couple of days, the overwhelming consensus, the overwhelming judgment, is that what we’ve done in this monetary medicine—it’s starting to work some, but there’s no firm conclusions.”

Later, Warsh said that the September boost to rates already had an effect on the tech sector. “You see market participants that are discriminating between the kinds of investments they want to make,” he said. Swaps now imply roughly 83% odds of a rate hike in December, down from around 95% prior to the Fed decision and Warsh’s remarks.

No one’s rooting for the Fed to keep pushing rates until credit markets buckle, and that’s why moving slowly makes sense. But the risk of a crunch is still extremely modest relative to the threat of entrenched inflation.

A government report Thursday [showed] that gross domestic product expanded at a strong 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter, and the S&P 500 Index is less than 1% from its all-time high. If Fed hikes managed to, say, take 10% to 20% off the stock market, the reverse wealth effect would primarily hit the wealthiest 10% of American households and have little direct effect on the bottom 50%, which suffers the most from inflation.

All of this supports the Fed’s case for pausing now, but a quarter-point rate increase in December is prudent at this point—a hike that’s already mostly priced into markets and would demonstrate Warsh’s commitment to restoring price stability.

Credit spreads would have to widen to the point that companies start to meaningfully revise capital expenditures expectations downward before markets think about pricing out a rate boost at year-end.

It’s not clear where Warsh stands on that matter, due to his general aversion to forward guidance. But if you believe the professional speculators in bond and derivatives markets, the subtle shakeout in the AI trade might already have caused Warsh to blink. ©Bloomberg

The author is a columnist focused on US markets and economics.

analysis.tldr: Changes in US Federal Reserve interest rates and the AI boom can shift foreign money flows, swaying Indian stock markets and the value of the rupee.
the_story: US Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh is an optimist who believes artificial intelligence will boost productivity and help vanquish inflation.
The Bloomberg Artificial Intelligence Index dropped up to 10% this month amid concerns over slowing revenue growth and rising borrowing costs for data centre companies.
The US Federal Reserve kept its interest rates steady at 3.75%-4%, while swaps now imply an 83% chance of a rate hike in December.
Meanwhile, the US economy expanded at a strong 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter, and inflation in the US has stayed above the Fed's 2% target for almost six years.
analysis.what_happened: US Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh faces questions about whether his strong optimism for artificial intelligence will trap him if the sector's funding stalls. The Fed recently kept interest rates steady at 3.75%-4% after a period of rate increases, causing bond markets to guess whether future rate hikes might pause due to tech sector wobbles.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local bank manager who loves a specific local industry and bets it will fix all community price rises, only to sweat when that industry hits a sudden cash crunch.
why_it_matters_india: US Federal Reserve signals on interest rates and tech sector health shift global investor confidence.
When US borrowing costs stay high or change, global investors (big foreign investors who invest in multiple countries) adjust where they park their money.
If foreign investors pull money out of emerging markets to chase safer US assets, it puts pressure on Indian financial markets.
This movement can ripple through to the rupee's exchange rate and local stock market performance.

impacts.rationale: Global tech sector wobbles and changing US interest rate expectations can cause foreign investors to pull money out, which usually hurts local stock indices—bad for Indian equity investors.
If US rate expectations shift or global risk appetite sours, the US dollar strengthens, making the rupee weaker (each rupee buys fewer dollars)—bad for importers and fuel buyers.
A slowdown or funding crunch in the US tech and artificial intelligence sector can reduce spending on software services, impacting Indian IT giants that serve US clients.

watch_next: The US Federal Reserve's official decision on whether to raise interest rates in December
Further earnings and funding updates from global artificial intelligence and cloud-computing companies
analysis.caveats: The article is an opinion column analyzing the mindset of a central bank chief, so actual Fed actions could differ from market speculations.

the_story: External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar criticized sanctions and shipping chokepoints for disrupting global energy trade and holding prices hostage.
He highlighted that unpredictability and significant disruptions are causing the current energy crisis, speaking during the G20 meeting.
Jaishankar called on the G20 to ensure energy markets remain open and predictable while highlighting India's efforts in critical minerals and reliable energy supplies.
analysis.what_happened: India's External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar spoke at the G20 meeting to criticize how sanctions and supply route blockages are disrupting global energy trade. This happened because geopolitical tensions and shipping bottlenecks are making oil supplies unpredictable and driving up uncertainty.
analysis.analogy: It is like a major neighborhood grocery supplier facing roadblocks and sudden fines, causing food prices in your local market to swing wildly up and down.
why_it_matters_india: Sanctions and shipping route bottlenecks create unpredictability in global oil supplies.
This uncertainty keeps global crude oil (raw petroleum) prices high or volatile.
Since India imports most of its oil, pricier imports raise domestic fuel and transport costs.
Higher transport costs ripple through the economy, pushing up inflation (the rate at which prices rise) for everyday goods.

impacts.rationale: Global disruptions make crude oil costlier, which is generally bad for regular people as it raises commuting and transport expenses.
Higher energy costs increase the price of moving goods across the country, making daily essentials more expensive — bad for household budgets.
Costlier oil imports mean India needs more US dollars to buy energy, which can weaken the local currency and make overall imports pricier.

events.headline: Federal Reserve Board releases results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families

items.title: Federal Reserve Board releases results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families
items.summary: Federal Reserve Board releases results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families

events.article_text:
An official website of the United States Government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock () or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Federal Reserve Board on Friday released the results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances, which provides the public and policymakers with detailed insights into the economic condition of American families.

The data provide a representative picture of what Americans own, how and how much they borrow, and how they bank. The current version of the survey has been undertaken every three years since 1989 and provides the public with an extensive time series of thorough information on the economic conditions of American families. Alongside the survey data, the Board issued its summary report entitled Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025 (PDF), which examines changes in income, net worth, assets, debt, and financial vulnerability.

In addition to the summary report, an interactive chartbook displaying changes in these financial characteristics over time is available here. Additional data from the survey, including extensive data examining other economic conditions of American families, is made available to researchers and the public here.

The survey is conducted for the Board by NORC, a social science research organization at the University of Chicago. Participants in the study are chosen at random from 119 geographic areas, including metropolitan areas and rural counties across the United States, using scientific sampling procedures that aim to produce a sample representative of American families.

For media inquiries, please email [email protected] or call (202) 452-2955.

Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025 Evidence from the Survey of Consumer Finances (PDF)

analysis.tldr: This U.S. consumer data survey tracks how American families handle money, which indirectly guides global interest rates and affects Indian markets.
the_story: The Federal Reserve Board released the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finances on Friday to show the economic condition of American families.
The survey covers what Americans own, how much they borrow, and how they bank, based on a representative sample conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago.
A summary report called Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025 details shifts in income, net worth, assets, debt, and financial vulnerability over the three-year period.
analysis.what_happened: The U.S. central bank published a major study detailing the financial health, debts, and savings of American households. This survey has been run every three years since 1989 to help policymakers understand how regular families are doing financially.
analysis.analogy: It is like a massive annual health check-up for a whole neighborhood, showing who is getting stronger and who is carrying too much weight.
why_it_matters_india: The Federal Reserve (America's central bank) studies how regular American families are spending and borrowing.
This data helps the Fed decide whether to raise or lower interest rates in the United States.
When U.S. interest rates change, global investors shift their money between countries like the U.S. and emerging markets like India.
This movement of money ultimately impacts foreign investments in Indian stock markets and the value of the Indian rupee.

impacts.rationale: If the survey data shows weak U.S. consumer health, the Fed might cut interest rates, pushing global money toward Indian stocks — which is generally good for Indian investors.
Softer U.S. economic data can weaken the dollar, helping the rupee buy more dollars — making imported goods slightly cheaper for India.

watch_next: Statements from U.S. Federal Reserve officials interpreting the survey results
Upcoming U.S. interest rate decisions tied to consumer health
analysis.caveats: The article text only mentions the release of a general survey without providing the specific statistical results, so the actual market impact depends entirely on what the raw data reveals.

events.article_text:
The third joint webinar by RUSI and War on the Rocks: Two leading defense publications from both sides of the Atlantic present their expert panel.

For this edition of The Atlantic Brief, the Royal United Services Institute and War on the Rocks present a dialogue on the future of trans-Atlantic defense cooperation following the U.S. midterm elections. Participating experts from the United Kingdom, continental Europe, and the United States bring decades of first-hand experience in the armed forces, diplomacy, and foreign policy.

analysis.tldr: A panel discussion by defense groups on U.S. election impacts on European security has no direct effect on your everyday finances, loans, or the prices you pay.
the_story: RUSI (Royal United Services Institute) and War on the Rocks hosted their third joint webinar called The Atlantic Brief.
The online event focused on the future of trans-Atlantic defense cooperation (military and strategic teamwork between North America and Europe) after the U.S. midterm elections.
The panel included experts from the United Kingdom, continental Europe, and the United States with backgrounds in the armed forces, diplomacy, and foreign policy.
analysis.what_happened: Two defense publications, RUSI and War on the Rocks, held an online panel discussion. The experts talked about how military and political cooperation between the United States and Europe might change following the U.S. midterm elections.
analysis.analogy: It is like a group of senior retired managers getting together on a video call to discuss how a change in company board members might affect overseas partnerships.
why_it_matters_india: Defense publications held a webinar on U.S. and European military cooperation -> This is a political and strategic discussion among Western experts -> It involves no trade, currency, or economic agreements -> Therefore, it creates no direct financial ripples for the Indian economy or retail investors.

impacts.rationale: Since this is just a foreign policy webinar with no economic data or trade policy changes, local stock markets will completely ignore it.
Currency values move based on money flows and interest rates, neither of which are touched by a defense policy discussion.

watch_next: Any actual policy changes or defense pacts signed by the U.S. or European governments that might affect global supply chains.
analysis.caveats: Only the headline and a very thin article description were available, confirming it is merely an event announcement rather than a financial or economic news report.

events.headline: Indian agri scientists find value in the use of iron ore tailings in farming

items.title: Indian agri scientists find value in the use of iron ore tailings in farming
items.summary: Initial experiments carried out by ICAR-IARI with tailings from ArcelorMittal Nippon Steel show higher yield, lower use of fertilizers

events.article_text:
Paddy being grown on soil mixed with iron ore tailings at an ArcelorMittal Nippon Steel site - Photo supplied by AMNS

“We will not see people calling iron ore tailings a waste anymore, and they will be thinking of converting them into value-added products and making money out of waste,” says Bhupinder Singh, Principal Scientist and Principal Investigator at ICAR-IARI (Indian Council of Agricultural Research-Indian Agriculture Research Institute).

Singh, who has been in agriculture research for over three-and-a-half decades, knows his onions.

His statement comes on the heels of a promising development with ICAR-IARI signing a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with ArcelorMittal Nippon Steel (AMNS) to conduct long-term research on the use of iron ore tailings in agriculture.

Bhupinder Singh, Principal Scientist and Principal Investigator at ICAR-IARI

Preliminary studies, done since 2024, have shown encouraging results of the use of iron ore tailings in the cultivation of paddy, wheat, and vegetables such as brinjal (eggplant) and lady’s finger (okra or bhindi). Results showed that the crop’s yield improved by 10-15 per cent, while use of chemical fertilizers was 20 per cent lower.

The signing of the long-term MoU comes after both organisations carried out studies for two years from 2024. The long-term MoU, which will run till 2029, will enable large-scale trials at ICAR-IARI and AMNS sites.

“In the second phase, we propose to work with different crops -cereals, oilseeds, non-edible flowers, tubers, particularly potato and vegetables. We can try agroforestry too by applying the tailings without affecting the soil quality,” he said.

The ICAR-IARI team first checked if valorisation of iron ore tailings from AMNS was feasible. Valorisation is turning mining waste into valuable secondary resources, reducing environmental hazards. Iron ore tailings cannot be applied directly to the soil since it may pollute it with other metals or even make it iron heavy.

“We used different organic amendments to reduce the total iron content of the tailings,” said Singh in an online interaction with businessline.

Singh’s team characterised iron ore tailings received from AMNS. The team found that they did not have any toxic heavy metals. “We characterised 6 batches. which were collected at different time intervals, because we wanted to be sure that our results are not based on one-time analysis,” he said.

It found the tailings rich in iron. “If the tailings are valorised, we can enrich them further with the various other macro and micronutrients. Based on the first phase, we have now entered into a long-term partnership with AMNS which will be on until 2029,” said Singh.

The valorised tailings are rich in iron, calcium, magnesium and many other elements which are required by the plants. Almost 12 per cent of cultivable lands in the country are iron deficient, and 49 per cent of soils are zinc deficient.

From the human nutrition point of view, the ICAR-IARI and AMNS project is trying to improve iron and zinc content in the crop, including through biofortification. “If a person requires to take iron daily, the crop will take care of dietary requirement,” he said.

The scientists’ team use biological consortia, a mix of bacteria and fungi which have the property of nutrient solubilisation. This is because most of the nutrients in the tailings are in oxide forms which are less soluble.

“We need to ensure that their availability is improved. We use different iron-solubilising bacteria which promote growth, chelating iron and zinc so that their uptake by the plant is ensured,” said Singh.

Experiments were conducted at the AMNS site, which has continuously been exposed to aerial precipitation of iron ore tailings.

“We planned some experiments at the AMNS site with different levels of iron ore tailings starting from 5-50 per cent of iron ore tailings mixed with soil. We have raised a few crops there until now, and we also tried some other products. Our results so far have been good,” said the ICAR-IARI principal scientist.

For two seasons, experiments at the AMNS site in Chhattisgarh were conducted with paddy. The team also tried brinjal and lady’s finger. “We have tried wheat in pots because we thought of not adding more, as many were sceptical,” he said.

Experiments at the AMNS site were on tiny plots. In the second phase, experiments will be carried out on ICAR-IARI pilots well, where the leaching behaviour of the tailings will be examined. “It will be a total environment impact assessment,” said Singh, adding that one of his students is doing a PhD programme working on the tailings impact on wheat and spinach.

ICAR-IARI conducted initial experiments in pots, working on a 600 kg per hectare formula, to ensure that if it takes it to the field, there will be no contamination. It was after this that the team decided to conduct its trials on AMNS sites.

He said tailings will be used in agriculture only after biological, physical and chemical valorisation. Physical processing will ensure proper mixing.

ICAR-IARI and AMNS would like to showcase this development to farmers, particularly around the latter’s sites.

During the second phase of the project, the focus will also be on addressing iron deficiency in soil and biofortification, he said, adding that large-scale trials will begin from November on ICAR-IARI plots.

“In addition, we will be conducting trials in Chhattisgarh, which is an organic state. We will use organic amendments of the tailings basically and avoid using any chemical,” said the ICAR-IARI scientist.

The trials will begin with batches of 10-20 farmers, maybe one or two farmers in each village, covering 10 villages.

analysis.tldr: Indian agricultural scientists have found that processed mining waste can boost crop yields while cutting chemical fertilizer use by 20%, which could eventually lower farming costs and improve soil health in India.
the_story: ICAR-IARI (Indian Council of Agricultural Research-Indian Agriculture Research Institute) signed a memorandum of understanding (an official partnership agreement) with ArcelorMittal Nippon Steel (AMNS) to run research until 2029.
Preliminary studies since 2024 showed that mixing treated iron ore tailings (mining waste) into soil improved crop yields by 10 to 15 per cent for paddy, wheat, brinjal, and lady's finger.
Using this treated waste reduced the need for chemical fertilizers by 20 per cent in early trials.
Scientists checked six batches of waste and confirmed they contain no toxic heavy metals, but are rich in iron, calcium, and magnesium.
The second phase of the project starts in November, expanding to large-scale trials on ICAR-IARI plots and with farmers in Chhattisgarh.
analysis.what_happened: Scientists at ICAR-IARI discovered that waste material left over from iron ore mining can be treated with organic amendments and bacteria to make it safe and nutritious for plants. After two years of successful small-scale trials on paddy, wheat, and vegetables at an AMNS site in Chhattisgarh, the two organizations signed a formal agreement to expand their research until 2029.
analysis.analogy: It is like discovering that the leftover peelings and scraps from food preparation, once safely composted, can act as a super-nutrient fertilizer for your home garden.
why_it_matters_india: Treating and using mining waste in farming -> reduces reliance on chemical fertilizers by 20%
Lower chemical fertilizer use -> cuts input costs for Indian farmers and reduces the government's massive fertilizer subsidy bill
Biofortification (adding nutrients to crops) using iron and zinc-rich tailings -> helps fight widespread soil and human nutritional deficiencies in India
Successful large-scale trials through 2029 -> could transform industrial waste into a valuable agricultural resource across mining-heavy states like Chhattisgarh

impacts.target: Fertiliser stocks (like Coromandel International, GNFC, or RCF)
impacts.rationale: If mining waste successfully replaces a portion of chemical fertilizers in the future, demand for commercial fertilizers could drop slightly, which is bad for fertilizer manufacturers.
Using processed waste instead of buying costly chemical fertilizers reduces expenses for farmers — which is good for rural incomes.

watch_next: The rollout of large-scale farmer trials in Chhattisgarh starting in November
Updates on whether the second phase successfully proves safety regarding soil leaching and environmental impact
analysis.caveats: These findings are still in the research and trial phase, and large-scale field results could differ from controlled site experiments.

events.article_text:
Eating disorders are on the rise. GLP-1s could make things worse.

GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade. But to some clinicians, they can represent something sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders.

A new report suggests the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up by 71% between 1990 and 2023. And clinicians are already seeing GLP-1s exacerbate the issue.

Here’s how they could make an already growing problem worse.

Used for decades in everything from nonstick pans to firefighting foams, PFAS, or “forever chemicals,” are linked to increased risks of fertility challenges, developmental delays, cancer, and reduced immune response.

Scrubbing PFAS-contaminated soil could eliminate a list of woes for people and planet. The concept is still in its infancy, but we can limit their buildup by pulling the chemicals out of water systems.

analysis.tldr: A massive global tech stock sell-off sparked by fears that artificial intelligence is hurting traditional search profits could ripple into Indian technology stocks.
the_story: Alphabet (Google's parent company) shed $500 billion in market value due to artificial intelligence taking a bite out of its search profits.
Amazon and Intel also furthered a wider fall in technology stocks.
Binance suffered the biggest crypto hack in history, affecting $6.3 billion in assets and leading to a suspension of all deposits and withdrawals.
Analysts blamed the Binance crypto hack on North Korea, and analysts believe the stolen Bitcoin will likely never be recovered.
analysis.what_happened: Major global technology giants saw massive drops in their market value, led by Alphabet losing $500 billion because artificial intelligence is changing how people search and threatening traditional advertising profits. At the same time, the crypto market was rattled by a record $6.3 billion hack on the Binance exchange, which forced the platform to freeze all customer money movements.
analysis.analogy: It is like a major shift in how people shop — say, everyone suddenly moving from local grocery stores to online delivery apps overnight, causing the grocery store's value to crash and making investors panic about the whole retail sector.
why_it_matters_india: Global tech stock sell-off occurs -> foreign investors grow nervous about high valuations in technology companies
Nervous foreign investors pull money out of emerging markets -> Indian stock markets face selling pressure
Indian IT (information technology) stocks like TCS and Infosys track global tech sentiment -> domestic tech shares drop in sympathy
Crypto hacks and tighter global sentiment -> Indian cryptocurrency investors face heightened fear and potential platform restrictions

impacts.rationale: Global tech crashes and panic often trigger foreign investors to pull money out of emerging markets like India, which can cause local indices to dip — generally bad for short-term investor portfolios.
When US tech giants struggle or suffer massive valuation drops, Indian software and technology export companies often fall in sympathy due to shared sentiment — bad for tech-focused investors.
The historic $6.3 billion Binance hack creates panic across the entire digital asset ecosystem, eroding trust and lowering crypto prices — bad for retail crypto holders.

watch_next: Whether the US tech stock sell-off continues or stabilizes
FIIs (big foreign investors) buying or selling trends in Indian markets
analysis.caveats: Global market sentiment can shift rapidly if upcoming company earnings reports or economic data surprise investors.

events.headline: New report looks at role of South-South and triangular cooperation for trade development

items.title: New report looks at role of South-South and triangular cooperation for trade development
items.summary: The growing importance of trade between developing economies - South-South trade - is highlighted in a joint publication launched on Day 1 (29 October) of the 10th Global Review of Aid for Trade by the WTO and the United Nations Office for South-South Cooperation (UNOSSC). The publication examines how the partnerships fostered through South-South cooperation and triangular cooperation – South-South partnerships supported by a developed economy - are helping strengthen developing economies' trade capacities and facilitate market access.

events.article_text:
Entitled "Transformative Partnerships for Trade Resilience: South-South and Triangular Cooperation in Action", the publication underscores that South-South merchandise exports reached USD 7.2 trillion in 2025, accounting for 27.8 per cent of world merchandise exports, compared with 14.3 per cent 20 years ago. South-South trade expanded 4.8-fold over this period, almost twice as fast as trade between developing and developed economies. However, trade remains heavily concentrated in Asian developing economies, while greater regional integration in Africa and Latin America and the Caribbean offers significant opportunities for further growth, the study finds.

South-South and triangular cooperation can help address trade barriers faced by developing economies by providing complementary channels for mobilizing knowledge, expertise and resources and by enabling developing economies to share relevant experience and solutions.

The publication presents six case studies of partnerships among developing economies, contributed by the Enhanced Integrated Framework (EIF) and the Standards and Trade Development Facility (STDF). These case studies illustrate how cooperation, supported by international organizations and development partners, can facilitate knowledge sharing, strengthen trade-related institutions, address regulatory constraints and improve market access in developing economies.

The publication explores the measurement and reporting of South-South cooperation. With contributions from United Nations Trade and Development (UNCTAD) and the International Forum on Total Official Support for Sustainable Development (TOSSD), hosted by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), it examines statistical frameworks that can help capture forms of development cooperation that complement Aid for Trade statistics, such as technical assistance, knowledge exchange and other non-financial contributions.

The publication underscores the importance of South-South and triangular cooperation in light of increasing pressure on traditional development assistance and underscores its role in complementing North-South cooperation. It identifies priorities for strengthening partnerships, improving coordination and measurement, and mobilizing additional expertise and resources to support trade and development.

In the launch session co-organized by the WTO, UNOSSC and Barbados, the WTO and UNOSSC reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening partnerships that help developing economies build trade capacity and benefit more fully from international trade.

The Ambassador of Barbados to the WTO, Matthew Wilson, who moderated the session, emphasized the growing importance of South-South and triangular cooperation. He called on the international community to explore ways to scale up these partnerships to help developing economies meet challenges, such as the digital transformation and strengthening resilience.

Participants also looked at opportunities to mobilize additional resources and expertise and improve the measurement of South-South cooperation.

The Director of UNOSSC, Dima Al-Khatib, said the publication is timely given the changing development cooperation landscape. She called for a "fresh look" at partnerships to broaden opportunities for achieving shared development goals, emphasizing the importance of stronger regional cooperation and enhanced coordination.

In his concluding remarks, WTO Deputy Director-General Xiangchen Zhang highlighted the importance of complementary forms of development cooperation amid growing pressure on traditional assistance. He said: "South-South and triangular cooperation is an important complement to traditional North-South cooperation. It brings additional expertise, resources and partnerships to support trade and development."

The full list of panellists can be found here.

analysis.tldr: A new global trade report shows developing countries are trading much more with each other, which could eventually open up new export markets and supply chains for India.
the_story: A new WTO report titled 'Transformative Partnerships for Trade Resilience' highlights that South-South merchandise exports reached USD 7.2 trillion in 2025.
This trade between developing economies now makes up 27.8 percent of global merchandise exports, up from 14.3 percent two decades ago.
The report notes that trade is currently concentrated in Asian developing economies, but regions like Africa and Latin America offer room for growth.
It also shares six case studies showing how developing countries share knowledge, expertise, and resources to tackle trade hurdles and regulatory issues.
analysis.what_happened: The World Trade Organization released a report detailing how trade among developing nations (known as South-South trade) has grown significantly, expanding 4.8-fold over the past twenty years. This growth is happening because developing countries are increasingly partnering, sharing knowledge, and helping each other overcome trade barriers as traditional financial aid faces growing pressure.
analysis.analogy: It is like a group of local neighborhood shops teaming up to share tips, buy supplies together, and help each other grow instead of relying solely on big department stores.
why_it_matters_india: Developing countries are increasingly trading among themselves rather than just with wealthy nations.
Asia is currently the center of this growing trade activity, where India is a major player.
Better regional partnerships and shared regulations can make it easier for Indian businesses to sell goods to other developing markets.
Over time, deeper trade ties among developing nations could help diversify where India buys and sells goods, reducing reliance on Western markets.

impacts.rationale: Indirectly, smoother trade and new markets for developing nations could help globally exposed Indian companies, which is generally good for investors.

watch_next: Further regional trade agreements involving developing nations
Updates on India's bilateral trade deals with African and Latin American countries
analysis.caveats: This report is an analytical study rather than a binding trade agreement, so its immediate impact on actual market prices is limited.

history.title: A budget that broke the pension system in three days
history.what: A new British government announced large unfunded tax cuts. Within three days UK government bond yields spiked so violently that pension funds faced collapse, and the Bank of England had to step in with emergency bond buying. The Prime Minister resigned within seven weeks.
history.why: Pension funds had used a strategy called liability-driven investing, which borrows against bonds to match long-term obligations. It works while yields move gradually. When yields jumped, the funds faced collateral calls, and the only way to meet them was to sell the very bonds that were falling — pushing yields higher still. Hidden leverage almost nobody outside the industry had noticed.
history.impact: The pound hit an all-time low against the dollar. Mortgage rates jumped and hundreds of mortgage products were pulled within days. The government's entire fiscal plan was reversed.
history.policy: The Bank of England bought long-dated bonds for a strictly limited window to break the loop, then regulators forced pension funds to hold far larger liquidity buffers against exactly this scenario.
history.consequence: It established that a rich, stable country with its own currency can still be disciplined by the bond market within days. Finance ministers everywhere became noticeably more careful about announcing unfunded spending.
history.pattern: The dangerous leverage is the leverage nobody discusses, usually because it sits inside an institution everyone considers boring. Ask who is forced to sell when prices fall — forced sellers turn a move into a spiral.
history.india_echo: India's fiscal deficit and government borrowing programme are worth watching for this reason. A bond market's patience is not infinite, and when it runs out it runs out in days rather than quarters.
history.watch_for: Bond yields rising while the currency falls. Normally higher yields support a currency; when both move the wrong way together, the market is questioning the government's credibility rather than its interest rates.
